# Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources

*Evidence briefing. Prepared for a working group on working-time policy.*

## Purpose

This briefing weighs five pieces of evidence on whether reducing the working week by a fifth, with pay maintained, raises productivity: the Halden multi-organisation pilot (source 1), the Varden County randomised trial at nine months (source 2), a re-analysis of the Halden pilot (source 3), a meta-analysis of 23 studies (source 4), and the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and of 14 Halden organisations (source 5). It adds no new data. Its aim is to state what the five together support, at the strength they support it, and what they leave open.

## 1. What each source contributes, and how later sources qualify it

**Source 1** established that many organisations that volunteered could cut scheduled hours by 20% with little change in reported output, and reported a 23.4% gain in output per hour, gains in every sector, large falls in sickness and resignations, and 92% continuation. Taken alone, it suggests a large, general effect.

**Source 2** was the first randomised evidence, with record-based output and actual hours. It introduced the distinction that the rest of the body depends on: between discretionary work, where output can be produced at any time within a deadline, and coverage-bound work, where output depends on presence while demand arrives. Per actual hour, output rose 12.5% in case-processing and 6.7% in counter work; per employee it was roughly unchanged in the first and fell 11.4% in the second. It also showed that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours, and that dividing by scheduled hours inflated the case-processing estimate from 12.5% to 22%.

**Source 3** found that source 1's figures were inflated in several documented ways: seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons, not "during the preparation phase"; manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points; actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%; and the 1.4% revenue rise was a real fall of about 2.6% after inflation of 4.1%. Correcting what could be corrected reduced the per-hour gain to 10.8% in a subset. These findings stand. Source 3 then went further, concluding that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact, attributing the remainder to novelty on the basis of an extrapolated survey trend, and dismissing source 2's meetings hypothesis as post hoc. Those further claims do not survive later evidence.

**Source 4** placed both studies in a wider literature. Its pooled per-hour estimate of 13.4% is inflated by the same features source 3 identified; the estimates from controlled designs (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and bias adjustment (+9.1%) converge on roughly 8 to 10%. Its work-type moderator generalises source 2: per-worker output fell about 9% in coverage-bound settings, consistently, and was roughly maintained in discretionary ones. It rejected source 1's sector-general claim and source 3's artifact claim. Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong, for the reason source 5 gives.

**Source 5** applied the strictest standards in the body: randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon. The per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours) but remained clearly above zero. Output per employee stood at −3.4%, with a confidence interval including zero. A registered mediation test attributed 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to reduced fatigue. Source 4's "no decay" conclusion rested on four long-follow-up studies, all uncontrolled and using scheduled hours. The counter arm was ended at month 12.

## 2. Weighing the estimates

**Table 1. Estimates of the change in output per hour, ordered by strength of design**

| Estimate | Source | Change per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | 1 | +23.4% |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | 5 | +11.8% |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | 3 | +10.8% |
| Meta-analysis, all studies | 4 | +13.4% |
| Meta-analysis, bias-adjusted | 4 | +9.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | 4 | +9.6% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 9 months, timesheets | 2 | +12.5% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 24 months, system logs | 5 | +8.5% |
| Randomised, counter work, 9 months | 2 | +6.7% |

Estimates fall as designs strengthen and stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work. The figure of more than 20% is not supported by any design that measures actual hours.

## 3. What the body supports

Read as a whole, the five sources support a conditional answer.

1. **Per hour, yes, by a moderate amount.** In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raises output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% under controlled measurement, with some decline from the first year to the second but no sign of disappearing within two years. The headline figure of more than 20% is an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
2. **Per worker, no.** Because actual hours fall by 11 to 14%, not 20%, a per-hour gain of 8 to 10% roughly offsets the hours cut but does not exceed it. Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 4% lower than it would have been, with intervals that include zero. "Same output in four days" is close to true there; "more output" is not supported.
3. **In coverage-bound work, the answer is no on any measure that matters to the people served.** Output per worker falls by about 9 to 11%, waits lengthen, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Per-hour gains exist but are small. This is the most consistent finding in the body.
4. **About half the per-hour gain in the best-measured setting comes from removing recurring meetings**, a smaller part from reduced fatigue, and about a third is unexplained.
5. **Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially** in every source that measured them (by roughly 27 to 36% for sick days). These are real benefits, but they are not themselves productivity, and the body does not estimate how far they offset per-worker output losses.

Whether "productivity" rises therefore depends on whether it is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output in a given role depends on presence. Both slogans, "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage", are wrong as stated.

## 4. What the body leaves open

- **Is the hours cut necessary for the gain?** About half the per-hour gain runs through cutting meetings. Two control offices that audited meetings without cutting hours saw a 4.1% per-hour rise, but that is two offices without a comparison group. No study had an arm that reorganised work without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and last, is not settled by this body.
- **Beyond two years.** No controlled evidence extends past 24 months. The per-hour gain declined between 9 and 24 months; whether it stabilises or continues to decline is unknown.
- **The unexplained third** of the per-hour gain has no tested mechanism.
- **Manufacturing and shift production** are almost absent from the evidence (two studies, both mixed).
- **Private-sector controlled evidence** is thin; the strongest designs are in public administration.

## 5. Bottom line

A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raises output per hour by roughly 8 to 10% in discretionary work, about half of it through fewer meetings, which roughly but not fully offsets the hours lost; in coverage-bound work it reduces output and service unless staff are added. Whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

</document>
response:
# Review: *Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources*

This is a good briefing. It describes each source accurately and states the conditional answer (per hour versus per worker, discretionary versus coverage-bound) clearly. It also gives the right verdicts on the two overclaims, "sector-general" and "entirely an artifact", and its list of open questions is well chosen.

Its main weakness is that it repeats several overstatements from the sources it relies on. The weaker steps in each source become flat statements of fact in the briefing:

- source 5's mixed-measure decline
- source 5's mediation, described as attributing the gain
- source 4's "convergence" of estimates
- the sickness figures

These matter most in the Bottom line, which is the part a working group will actually read. The briefing also leaves out cost, which is the outcome policy-makers most need.

## 1. Accuracy against the sources

**Figures repeated from the sources.** I checked these against the sources: 23.4, 12.5/22, 6.7, −11.4, 10.8, 3.8 points, 14.1%, −2.6% real, 13.4, 8.2, 7.9, 9.7, 9.6, 9.1, −3.4, 47/18, and the four uncontrolled long-follow-up studies. All match.

**Statements that misstate or overstate the sources:**

- **"Declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours)"** compares different measures. 12.5% is the 9-month figure on timesheets; 8.5% is the 24-month figure on system logs. The like-for-like comparison is **12.5% to 9.8%**, a fall of about a fifth, not a third. Source 5's own Section 5 uses the like-for-like figure.
- **The decline omits contamination.** Two control offices ran their own meeting audits from month 15. That probably accounts for part of the apparent fade, roughly 1 of the 2.7 points. A sentence on this belongs wherever the decline is mentioned.
- **"Source 4's claim … was wrong."** Source 5 showed the claim was *unsupported*: the four long studies cannot speak to decay. It is shown wrong only to the extent that one controlled trial with 7 offices per arm found some decline. "Unsupported" is the accurate word.
- **Source 1's 92% continuation** is reported without its most informative detail. All five reversions came from retail and hospitality and from healthcare administration, which is the work-type pattern the rest of the body confirms.

## 2. Table 1 is not ordered as claimed

The table is labelled "ordered by strength of design", but it is not:

- The meta-analysis's all-studies estimate (+13.4%) sits below two uncontrolled subsets.
- Randomised counter work (+6.7%) is a different type of work, but appears as if it were the strongest-design row.

The data also do not fall steadily as design strengthens:

- The randomised 9-month estimate (+12.5%) is higher than every meta-analysis subgroup.
- The uncontrolled source 5 estimate (+11.8%) is lower than the meta-analysis pooled figure.

Part of the move toward 8–10% reflects duration and measurement (the 24-month figure on logs), not design alone.

**Suggested fix:** split the table by work type, then order within each part by design. Change "Estimates fall as designs strengthen" to "Estimates are broadly lower under stronger designs."

## 3. Claims stated more firmly than the evidence allows

**"Converge on roughly 8 to 10%."** The meta-analysis subgroups overlap heavily. Most of the actual-hours and record-based studies are also the controlled ones. Their agreement is therefore largely one signal counted several times. In addition, the trim-and-fill adjustment may be picking up the same design effect rather than publication bias. The 8–10% range is still reasonable, but it rests mainly on:

- one randomised trial (Varden, about +8.5–10% at 24 months), and
- one set of overlapping meta-analysis subgroups.

**"About half the per-hour gain … comes from removing recurring meetings"** (point 4 and the Bottom line). This is the weakest claim promoted to the headline. Several open issues sit behind it:

- The registered test used the same 14 offices whose month-6 data generated the hypothesis.
- With seven treated offices, the effective sample is small. The confidence interval is 28–66%.
- Mediator–outcome confounding is plausible. For example, better-run offices may both cut more meetings and improve output more.
- It is unclear what the log-hours outcome measures. If it records case time only, a "meetings" pathway means improved focus, not simply the removal of low-value time.

**Suggested wording:** "A registered test in one trial attributes roughly half (28–66%) of the per-hour gain to fewer recurring meetings. This is the best-supported mechanism, but it has not been independently replicated."

**"Maintaining service requires about 12% more staff"** (point 3). This is the county's estimate, derived from output per employee. In demand-driven work, waiting times depend on staffed hours. Restoring them is likely to need closer to **15–20%** more staff, depending on how much of the per-hour gain is real capacity rather than less idle time. Present 12% as a lower bound.

**Sickness and resignations** (point 5). There are three problems with "fall substantially in every source … These are real benefits":

- In the meta-analysis, only 14 of 23 studies reported sick leave. That pattern is consistent with selective reporting.
- None of the sources standardised sick days for fewer scheduled working days. Part of the fall may be mechanical, if the change was implemented as a four-day week.
- Source 1's −36% is uncontrolled and not adjusted for season.

**Suggested wording:** "Recorded sickness absence and resignations fall in every study that reports them; part of the sickness fall may reflect fewer scheduled working days, which no source has adjusted for."

## 4. A small arithmetic inconsistency in point 2

The briefing gives a per-hour gain of 8–10% and an hours reduction of 11–14%. Combined, these imply output per worker between about **−2% and −7%**:

- 1.10 × 0.89 ≈ 0.98
- 1.08 × 0.86 ≈ 0.93

The stated range of "2 to 4% lower" matches the direct estimates (−2.1%, −2.7% and −3.4%), but it does not follow from the briefing's own component ranges. Either cite the direct estimates explicitly or widen the range.

The point-1 phrase "a 20% cut" is also slightly loose. The meta-analysis pooled cuts of 10% or more and did not adjust for the size of the cut. Varden was the only 20% cut with controlled evidence.

## 5. Omitted: cost

For a working-time policy group, the most decision-relevant result is unit labour cost, and none of the five sources nor the briefing states it.

- **Discretionary work:** pay is unchanged and output per worker is about 3% lower. Cost per unit of output therefore rises about **3%**, plus any paid overtime. Varden case-processing staff averaged about 3 hours a week of claimed overtime.
- **Coverage-bound work:** cost per contact rises **9% or more** if staff are added to restore service. As noted in section 3, this is probably an understatement.

Against these costs, the benefits from lower sickness and turnover are real but unquantified. A short paragraph setting out this trade-off would make the briefing much more useful. It should also be added to "what the body leaves open": no source estimates whether lower absence and turnover recover the extra cost.

## 6. Additions to "What the body leaves open"

- **Size of the cut.** There is no evidence on cuts other than about 20% under controlled conditions, so it is unknown whether a 10% cut gives proportionally similar results.
- **Deadline-driven client work.** The source 5 marketing agency reverted because of client deadlines. That case fits neither the discretionary nor the coverage-bound category and may need its own.
- **Statistical precision.** The randomised estimates rest on 7 offices per arm. Few-cluster inference was never reported, so the true confidence intervals may be wider than shown.
- **The design that would settle the main open question:** a three-arm trial comparing an hours cut, a meeting audit only, and a control group.

## 7. Suggested revision of the Bottom line

> A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay reduces actual hours by about 11–14% and, in discretionary work, raises output per actual hour by roughly 8–10%. That gain has faded somewhat but persisted over two years in the one randomised trial. Output per worker ends up about 2–4% lower, so cost per unit of output rises modestly. The best-supported mechanism is fewer recurring meetings, though this rests on a single trial. In coverage-bound work, output and service fall unless staff are added, at a cost of at least 9% per contact. Sickness absence and resignations fall, but their value has not been set against these costs. Whether the gain requires cutting hours, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

With those changes, the briefing would match the evidence closely. Its overall structure and its central conditional answer need no change.
